newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish one-day depos soar to lombard rate.
newsitem.headline: Polish one-day depos soar to lombard rate.

text.p: Polish one-day deposit rates surged more than one point and hit the 25-percent lombard rate as the money market was sqeezed by banks' squaring monthly reserve accounts and cash withdrawls ahead of Easter holiday.

One-day rates were seen remaining around the lomard rate for the rest of the week as some banks desperately searched for funds and those with surpluses were reluctant to cut positions, wary of negative balances during the three-day Easter break.
"Big banks are reluctant to lend funds despite high rates because they are protecting their positions," said Krzysztof Chmura from Bank Gdanski SA.
At 0920 GMT overnight deposit rates were at 24.60/25.20 percent, up from 23.30/23.60 at opening and tomorrow/next rates were at 24.60/25.40 percent, up from opening's 23.35/23.65.
The last working day to square average reserve positions is Friday, but the March reserve period ends on Monday.

The zloty inched down against the basket of currencies in early trade amid a light currency-buying trend on the back of importers orders but the trade was seen generally subdued ahead of the holiday break with no foreign interest expected.

At 0930 GMT the zloty was quoted at 2.94/2.91 percent from the trading band centre, weaker from 3.00/2.92 at opening. It was at 3.0788/98 to the dollar, down from opening's 3.0760/80 and at 1.8299/04 to the mark, against 1.8295/15.

Foreign investors were seen taking a stand-by stance after the Finance Minister said the current pace of zloty devaluation was favourable for exporters and that there was no need for a deeper depreciation despite a growing trade gap.
The zloty, now devaluated one percent per month against a basket of five western currencies, is expected to surpass its 1997 target devaluation of nine percent for this year.
Dealers said the statement was in line with market views as the central bank was expected to keep the zloty stable in order to keep foreigners from buying large amounts of local currency instruments.

"The central bank is not likely to cut the crawl rate amid growing interest rates, because it would trigger an inflow of speculative investment, which would have to be additionally sterilised," said an analyst at a foreign company here.
